extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), respondents in USPTO disciplinary proceedings, and USPTO enrollment & discipline officials
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures the USPTO applies when imposing reciprocal discipline based on a state disciplinary adjudication under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24, including the Selling v. Radford elements a respondent must rebut. Also describes sanctions and procedural relief the Office will order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicate for reciprocal discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation of 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(h) — being suspended on ethical grounds by a duly constituted authority of a State — is the predicate for imposing reciprocal discipline before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED Director may request the USPTO Director to impose reciprocal discipline where a practitioner has been suspended by a state; the Final Order here was issued pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 predicated upon such a state suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling presumption (state discipline creates federal presumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: A state disbarment or suspension creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of reciprocal discipline is proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Selling v. Radford, the USPTO presumes the appropriateness of identical reciprocal discipline unless the respondent clearly and convincingly establishes one of the Selling elements (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)). The USPTO is not a forum to re-litigate the state proceeding; federal review is narrow and deferential.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(i) — Deprivation of due process
rubrics_metrics.description: [T]he procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To defeat reciprocal discipline on this ground, respondent must show by clear and convincing evidence a genuine issue of material fact that the out-of-state proceeding deprived him of the fundamental requirement of due process (meaningful opportunity to be heard). Indicators of proper due process include reasonable notice of charges, attendance and active participation at hearings, representation by counsel, ability to present evidence, testify, cross-examine witnesses, and make arguments (citing Mathews v. Eldridge; Ruffalo; In re Squire; In re Zdravkovich). Mere allegations about limited roles of investigative panels or disagreement with findings do not satisfy this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(ii) — Infirmity of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: [T]here was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must show more than disagreement with factfinding; he must demonstrate a 'such an infirmity of proof' that accepting the state conclusion would be inconsistent with the Office's duty. This is a difficult, narrow showing. Deference is given to the trier-of-fact's credibility determinations; relitigation of credibility does not ordinarily demonstrate infirmity (citing In re Zdravkovich and case law). Core undisputed facts supporting state findings strongly undercut an infirmity claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii) — Grave injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: [T]hat the imposition of the same public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grave injustice analysis focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct. Courts/USPTO inquire whether the sanction was so ill-fitted to the adjudicated misconduct that reciprocal discipline would be unjust. Consider whether the sanction is within the appropriate range, whether aggravating/mitigating factors were considered, and whether the state's sanction was rationally based. Disagreement over sanction severity (e.g., state imposed 120 days vs. recommended 90 days) will not typically establish grave injustice if the state carefully weighed factors and the sanction was authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iv) — Public discipline argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subsection (as printed in the Final Order) appears as the statutory enumerant; a respondent may raise arguments related to whether public discipline was in fact imposed. The respondent still bears the burden of showing a genuine issue of material fact by clear and convincing evidence to avoid reciprocal discipline under the regulation's listed grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent's burden and standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent must demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that one of the Selling elements precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal precedent (e.g., In re Kramer; In re Friedman) establishes that the respondent attorney bears the burden by clear and convincing evidence. The USPTO applies this narrow and deferential standard and will not act as a court of review to discover error in the state courts' proceedings (citing Zdravkovich; Sibley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process — specific indicators that satisfy the requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Due process in disciplinary proceedings is satisfied where the respondent received reasonable notice of charges and had an opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete indicators include: attendance and active participation in hearings, representation by counsel, opportunity to present evidence and exhibits, to testify, to call and cross-examine witnesses, to make objections and arguments, and to pursue appeals. Mere assertions about potential appearances of impropriety in preliminary investigative panels that did not participate in final decisionmaking generally do not show deprivation of due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to state factfindings; narrow review of credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO gives deference to the state tribunal's findings of fact and credibility determinations in reciprocal-discipline cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disagreement about the credibility of witnesses or the weighing of evidence does not ordinarily show an infirmity of proof. The Office will accept undisputed core facts supporting the state findings unless respondent makes the difficult showing required to overcome deference (citing In re Zdravkovich and related authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice — proportionality and sanction-range review
rubrics_metrics.description: To show 'grave injustice,' respondent must show the punishment imposed by the state was so disproportionate to the misconduct that imposing identical discipline would be unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the sanction was within the range authorized, whether the state court considered aggravating and mitigating factors, and whether the state imposed sanction was reached after full process. Case law indicates that sanctions within the appropriate range and reached after considered process do not constitute grave injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO procedural requirements when imposing discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: When the USPTO imposes reciprocal discipline the Office will take specific procedural actions and issue orders consistent with 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 and related rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical orders include: suspending the respondent from practice before the USPTO for the identical period; publishing Notice of Suspension in the Official Gazette (with specified content); giving notice pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.59 to state disciplinary agencies and courts; directing compliance with duties in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58; dissociating respondent's name from Customer Numbers and PKI certificates; prohibiting application for or association with USPTO Customer Numbers until reinstatement; and any other relief the nature of the cause requires. The Notice should summarize the misconduct and the state findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of state-law determinations and federal preemption limits
rubrics_metrics.description: State disciplinary authorities retain control over attorney regulation within their borders even for conduct occurring before federal tribunals; federal patent/other federal law generally does not preempt state discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent (Sperry; Kroll v. Finnerty; Gadda v. Ashcroft) supports that state courts may discipline attorneys for conduct in federal matters and that the USPTO may rely on state discipline absent compelling preemption arguments. Arguments that state discipline was premature because related federal litigation remained pending are generally unpersuasive absent clear preemption or due process defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior disciplinary and judicial decisions as guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO (and respondent) should look to federal and D.C. Circuit precedent and prior reciprocal-discipline decisions for interpretation and application of the Selling elements and § 11.24.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order cites Selling v. Radford; In re Kramer; In re Friedman; In re Zdravkovich; In re Sibley; In re Squire; In re Nace (D.C. Cir. decisions) as authorities illustrating the narrow standard of review, burden of proof, and application of the Selling criteria. These cases explain that USPTO review is deferential and focused on whether a genuine issue of material fact exists under the regulatory elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of misconduct supporting reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific factual bases the state found sufficient to discipline (examples of misconduct): failing to keep a client informed, failing to safeguard property, acting dishonestly, lacking competence and diligence, and conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this matter the West Virginia Supreme Court found respondent violated West Virginia Rules 1.1 (competence), 1.3 (diligence), 1.4(a) and (b) (communication), 1.15(b) (safekeeping property), 8.4(c) (dishonesty), and 8.4(d) (conduct prejudicial to administration of justice) by (among other things) forming an attorney-client relationship with the bankruptcy trustee, returning funds to the original client rather than the trustee, and failing to keep the trustee informed. Such core facts supported the state's 120-day suspension and were considered by the USPTO in imposing identical discipline.
